title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 15–16
description: Reviewed B2 vocabulary for university courses and qualifications, academic settings and funding, workplace roles, jobs, trades, working conditions and career changes.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study using the user-provided book. Teaching topics and lexical targets are source-grounded; explanatory notes, examples and Brazilian Portuguese translations are newly authored.

audit.scope: Teaching pages, pictures/captions, language-help and common-mistakes boxes, exercises 15.1–15.5 and 16.1–16.6, and corresponding answer-key entries.
audit.pronunciation: Conservative broad British IPA is included for reliably transcribed individual words; many multiword targets have empty IPA to avoid guesswork on connected speech.
audit.languagePolicy: All study fields in English except Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Checked source teaching pages and exercises with the relevant answer-key section; checked schema, unique IDs, originals examples, short vocabulary audio targets and empty audio assets. No live VocabLab browser test.
audit.limitations: No bundled recordings. Browser import, speech recognition and text-to-speech have not been tested.

units.title: Unit 15 — Higher education
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 36–37 (PDF pages 37–38).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: Education: UK degrees, campus teaching and student support
learningObjectives: Distinguish undergraduate, graduate and postgraduate students, and bachelor’s, master’s and PhD qualifications.
Describe degree programmes, credits, modules, dissertation and thesis in UK higher education.
Name teaching formats and university locations: lectures, seminars, tutorials, campus and halls of residence.
Discuss applications, entry requirements, tuition fees, loans, scholarships and student unions.

sectionsChecked: B: People, places, and types of classes; Language help
C: Student services (admissions, funding, student union)

items.pt: estudos de graduação; formação universitária inicial
items.example: Undergraduate studies helped her develop practical skills in biology.
items.note: The first stage of university education, usually leading to a bachelor's degree.

items.example: As an undergraduate, he joined a research group.
items.note: A student working towards their first university degree; often shortened to undergrad.

items.example: The university runs workshops for new undergrads.
items.note: Informal shortened noun for undergraduate; not a graduate who has finished their degree.

items.example: She earned a bachelor's degree in mechanical engineering.
items.note: A first university degree; the apostrophe and s are standard in bachelor's degree.

items.example: The university offers a three-year programme in economics.
items.note: British university term for an organised course of study; US spelling often program.

items.example: The robotics module includes a practical laboratory project.
items.note: A component of a wider university programme; do not treat it as the whole degree.

items.example: This optional module is worth fifteen credits.
items.note: Academic units measuring completed coursework; credit counts vary by institution.

items.example: To complete the module, students must submit two assignments.
items.note: Complete means finish all required work, not merely attend a class.

items.example: Her dissertation examines how renewable energy affects small communities.
items.note: In this book's UK context, often a substantial written project for a bachelor's or master's degree; usage varies by system.

items.example: The final project is worth thirty credits.
items.note: Worth specifies how much academic credit a module or project counts for.

items.example: He hopes to graduate next summer.
items.note: Verb: complete a degree; in BrE it commonly takes from a university or with a degree.

items.example: The company is recruiting graduates with programming experience.
items.note: Noun for someone who has already completed a university degree; contrasts with undergraduate.

items.example: Postgraduate studies usually involve more specialised research.
items.note: Higher-level university study after an initial degree.

items.example: The postgraduate presented her findings at a conference.
items.note: A student pursuing a master's degree or PhD; also used as an adjective.

items.example: Several postgrads attended the departmental meeting.
items.note: Informal shortened form of postgraduate student.

items.example: She is studying for a master's degree in data science.
items.note: A postgraduate degree, normally below a PhD; do not confuse master's with a job title.

items.pt: doutorado; título de doutor em pesquisa
items.example: He completed a PhD in materials science.
items.note: The research doctorate called Doctor of Philosophy; the field need not be philosophy.

items.example: Her doctorate focused on medical imaging.
items.note: General noun for a doctoral-level qualification; PhD is one type.

items.example: During her master's degree, she decided to specialise in robotics.
items.note: Use specialise in + subject or field; British spelling has -ise.

items.pt: área de conhecimento; campo de atuação
items.example: Her field is environmental engineering.
items.note: Here field means an academic or research discipline, not a physical field.

items.example: Our laboratory does research into new sensors.
items.note: Research is uncountable in this academic sense: do research, not do researches.

items.example: The team is conducting research into energy storage.
items.note: Research into something is a common academic pattern.

items.example: His doctoral thesis explains the proposed communication architecture.
items.note: The book uses thesis mainly for PhD-level work and dissertation for other degrees; naming varies internationally.

items.pt: campus universitário; conjunto de instalações da universidade
items.section: B · People, places and types of classes
items.example: The university campus includes libraries and engineering laboratories.
items.note: Campus describes the university site, not one individual classroom.

items.pt: no campus; dentro da área universitária
items.section: B · People, places and types of classes
items.example: Many international students live on campus.
items.note: Common phrase for being or living on the university grounds.

items.section: B · People, places and types of classes
items.example: The guest speaker addressed two hundred students in the lecture theatre.
items.note: In British English, a large room with rows of seats used for university lectures.

items.section: B · People, places and types of classes
items.example: The lecture hall was full for the introductory physics class.
items.note: An alternative to lecture theatre in this context.

items.section: B · People, places and types of classes
items.example: We have a lecture on control systems every Tuesday.
items.note: Typically a large-group teaching session; can also mean a formal talk.

items.pt: docente universitário; professor que ministra aulas
items.section: B · People, places and types of classes
items.example: A lecturer explained the method before the laboratory session.
items.note: A university teacher; the term is not always equivalent to a full professor in academic rank.

items.section: B · People, places and types of classes
items.example: I take notes during lectures so I can review the main ideas later.
items.note: Natural collocation; take notes when recording information; make notes is also acceptable.

items.pt: seminário; aula em grupo para discussão
items.section: B · People, places and types of classes
items.example: In the seminar, students compared two approaches to the problem.
items.note: Usually a smaller session focused on discussion; contrasts with a lecture.

items.section: B · People, places and types of classes
items.example: Academic staff discussed the changes to the curriculum.
items.note: Collective expression for university teachers and researchers; staff as a collective noun.

items.pt: tutor; orientador acadêmico; docente que acompanha estudantes
items.section: B · People, places and types of classes
items.example: Her tutor gave detailed feedback on the project proposal.
items.note: Someone who teaches or supports students individually or in smaller groups.

items.pt: aula tutorial; sessão de orientação em grupo pequeno
items.section: B · People, places and types of classes
items.example: The tutorial gave everyone a chance to ask questions.
items.note: A session involving close contact with a tutor; not simply a video tutorial in this context.

items.section: B · People, places and types of classes
items.example: First-year students can apply for a room in halls of residence.
items.note: British university accommodation, often shortened to halls.

items.section: B · People, places and types of classes
items.example: She spent her first year living in halls.
items.note: Short form of halls of residence in UK student English.

items.pt: setor de admissões; processo de ingresso
items.example: Admissions will confirm whether your application is complete.
items.note: In this context, the university department responsible for applications and new students.

items.example: The admissions office answered questions about the entry process.
items.note: Handles applications and entry, not student-union activities.

items.pt: candidatar-se a um programa de estudos
items.example: You can apply for the programme through the university website.
items.note: Apply for + programme or course; apply to + university is also common.

items.pt: requisitos de ingresso; pré-requisitos de admissão
items.example: Check the entry requirements before choosing a postgraduate course.
items.note: Qualifications or conditions you must meet to be admitted; not tuition payments.

items.example: Applicants must submit an application by the end of March.
items.note: Submit means formally send an application for consideration.

items.example: Her application included a statement of academic interests.
items.note: In this context, a formal request to enter a course.

items.example: The university provides funding for some research projects.
items.note: Money available to support study or research; not the same as a tuition fee.

items.example: Tuition fees are considerably higher for some international students.
items.note: Money charged for teaching on a course; systems differ across countries.

items.example: The academic year begins in September at many UK universities.
items.note: A teaching year at a school or university, not necessarily January to December.

items.example: She used a student loan to help pay her course fees.
items.note: Borrowed money that generally has to be repaid; contrasts with a scholarship.

items.example: He was awarded a scholarship for his research achievements.
items.note: Financial support that normally does not require repayment, unlike a loan.

items.pt: candidatar-se a uma bolsa de estudos
items.example: She will apply for a scholarship before accepting the offer.
items.note: Use apply for when requesting financial support or funding.

items.pt: união estudantil; entidade representativa dos estudantes
items.example: The student union organised a debate about campus transport.
items.note: The university organisation representing students and supporting student life.

items.example: Student societies organise activities outside formal classes.
items.note: Groups built around interests or shared activities, rather than academic modules.

items.example: He joined a student club focused on public speaking.
items.note: A group for a shared activity or interest, similar to a student society.

items.example: A bachelor's degree is usually considered a first degree.
items.note: Another label for the initial university degree, before postgraduate study.

items.example: The research project required both experiments and a written report.
items.note: Exercise context reinforces research as academic investigation.

items.example: She hopes to complete her PhD within four years.
items.note: The exercise asks learners to use the field and PhD vocabulary in context.

units.title: Unit 16 — Work
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 38–39 (PDF pages 39–40).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: Employment: workplace roles, trades, work schedules and career changes
learningObjectives: Use job as a countable position noun and work as an uncountable activity noun.
Name workplace roles and distinguish professions from skilled manual trades.
Use collocations for earning a living, finding employment and taking on a job.
Differentiate shift work, flexi-time, industrial action, dismissal, redundancy and leave.
Use common career expressions such as be promoted, take early retirement and apply for a job.

sectionsChecked: A: Jobs in a workplace; Common mistakes (job versus work)
B: Trades and professions; profession and trade illustration
C: Collocations of words connected with work

items.example: A director voted on the company's long-term strategy.
items.note: A member of the board or leadership; not necessarily the person who supervises daily tasks.

items.example: The executive approved the proposed investment.
items.note: A senior decision-maker; not interchangeable with administrator.

items.example: The administrator coordinates office schedules and routine procedures.
items.note: Focuses on the day-to-day running of an organisation or department.

items.example: A skilled worker repaired the damaged control panel.
items.note: A worker trained for tasks needing specific abilities; contrasts with unskilled worker.

items.example: The factory initially hired unskilled workers for basic packing tasks.
items.note: The book uses the traditional term for jobs needing little formal training; its use can be sensitive today.

items.example: The receptionist checked the visitor's name and issued a badge.
items.note: A person who receives visitors or answers initial enquiries.

items.example: The public relations officer prepared a statement for journalists.
items.note: Manages communication with the public and media.

items.example: A union representative met managers to discuss working conditions.
items.note: A worker representative in discussions about employees' interests.

items.example: A researcher tested new materials in the laboratory.
items.note: Investigates questions or develops products; can work inside a company.

items.example: The supervisor checked that the assembly tasks were being completed safely.
items.note: Oversees other workers' day-to-day work.

items.example: The board of directors reviewed the annual report.
items.note: The book defines director by membership of the board; this phrase makes the relationship explicit.

items.section: A · Job and work: common mistakes
items.example: She got a new job as a mechanical engineer.
items.note: Countable noun for a particular position: a job, two jobs; contrast uncountable work.

items.section: A · Job and work: common mistakes
items.example: There is plenty of work to finish before Friday.
items.note: Uncountable noun for tasks or activities; do not say a work for an individual employment position.

items.section: A · Job and work: common mistakes
items.example: I usually get to work before eight.
items.note: Work here means the workplace; the book explicitly warns against get to job.

items.section: A · Job and work: common mistakes
items.example: He got a new job after moving to the city.
items.note: Use a job for a specific role or position, rather than a work.

items.section: A · Job and work: common mistakes
items.example: Developing safety-critical software can be demanding work.
items.note: Demanding means requiring effort or skill; work is not counted here.

items.example: Law is a profession that requires substantial training.
items.note: The book contrasts professions requiring qualifications with skilled manual trades.

items.pt: servidor público; funcionário do serviço público
items.example: The civil servant helped implement a new transport policy.
items.note: Works in government administration; not necessarily an elected politician.

items.example: The scientist developed a method for measuring air quality.
items.note: A person professionally involved in scientific investigation.

items.example: The designer created a more accessible user interface.
items.note: Listed under both professions and trades in the source diagram: depends on the work and training.

items.example: The judge explained the decision in court.
items.note: The legal professional who makes decisions in court cases.

items.example: The lecturer supervises students' final projects.
items.note: A university teacher; also appears in Unit 15.

items.example: A physiotherapist helped her recover from a knee injury.
items.note: Health professional working with movement and physical rehabilitation.

items.example: The ambassador attended the diplomatic reception.
items.note: Represents a government abroad in a senior diplomatic role.

items.example: The economist studied changes in regional employment.
items.note: A professional who analyses economic activity and data.

items.example: The banker advised the company on financing options.
items.note: A person who works professionally in banking.

items.example: Plumbing is a trade that requires specialist practical skills.
items.note: The unit contrasts skilled manual trades with professions; trade has other meanings elsewhere.

items.example: A firefighter inspected the damaged building after the fire.
items.note: A person trained to control fires and help during emergencies.

items.pt: cuidador ou cuidadora de crianças em domicílio
items.example: The childminder looks after three children during working hours.
items.note: In British usage, often someone who cares for other people's children in their own home.

items.example: The carpenter built a wooden frame for the new window.
items.note: Skilled trade involving woodwork and construction.

items.example: The plumber repaired a leaking pipe beneath the sink.
items.note: Skilled person working with water supply and pipes; the b is silent.

items.example: It can be difficult to get work without recent experience.
items.note: Work is uncountable here, so avoid get a work.

items.example: She managed to find work soon after graduating.
items.note: Refers to finding paid activity in general, not necessarily one specific job.

items.example: He was offered a job in the software team.
items.note: The verb offer works with both a job and work in different contexts.

items.example: She was offered work on a short-term research project.
items.note: Work may refer to paid assignments without a distinct permanent position.

items.pt: para ganhar a vida; como meio de sustento
items.example: What do you do for a living?
items.note: The fixed question asks about someone's paid occupation; also earn or make a living.

items.example: He works in publishing and reviews technical manuscripts.
items.note: Use work in for an industry or field; also work in banking, design or education.

items.example: After university, she started working in banking.
items.note: Industry preposition: in banking, not at banking.

items.example: She makes a living by translating scientific papers.
items.note: Means earn enough to support oneself; not the same as become wealthy.

items.example: He makes a living as a freelance editor.
items.note: Use make a living as + occupation or by + activity.

items.example: As a freelance writer, she works for several clients.
items.note: Freelance means working independently rather than permanently for one employer.

items.pt: assumir um trabalho; aceitar uma responsabilidade profissional
items.example: He agreed to take on a difficult job at short notice.
items.note: Take on emphasises agreeing to responsibility; different from merely finding a vacancy.

items.pt: horário de trabalho; jornada de trabalho
items.example: Her hours of work change during the busy season.
items.note: Refers to the hours a person is expected to work.

items.example: Some hospital staff do shiftwork overnight.
items.note: Shiftwork is often written as shift work; work shifts is another option.

items.example: Technicians work shifts to keep the system running all night.
items.note: The schedule alternates between working periods rather than fixed office hours.

items.example: The shift worker has to adjust his sleep schedule regularly.
items.note: The Unit 16 answer key also uses shiftworker as one word for a person who works shifts.

items.example: She is on flexi-time and can start earlier if needed.
items.note: BrE work arrangement allowing some choice over when to work.

items.example: He works nine-to-five and rarely stays late.
items.note: A conventional daytime pattern, approximately 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

items.example: After years of night shifts, she wanted a nine-to-five job.
items.note: An ordinary daytime work schedule; figurative when referring to a routine office job.

items.section: C · Not working and employment changes
items.example: The employees decided to go on strike after negotiations failed.
items.note: An organised stop in work during an industrial dispute.

items.section: C · Not working and employment changes
items.example: The drivers have been on strike since Monday.
items.note: State of participating in a strike; contrast the action go on strike.

items.pt: conflito trabalhista; disputa entre empregados e empregadores
items.section: C · Not working and employment changes
items.example: The company and union held talks to resolve the industrial dispute.
items.note: Formal labour-relations term for disagreement between workers and management.

items.section: C · Not working and employment changes
items.example: He got the sack after repeatedly ignoring safety rules.
items.note: Informal British expression for being dismissed from a job; often suggests fault.

items.section: C · Not working and employment changes
items.example: She was fired for serious misconduct.
items.note: An ordinary expression for employer-initiated dismissal, not usually for redundancy.

items.section: C · Not working and employment changes
items.example: The manager was dismissed after an internal investigation.
items.note: The Unit 16 answer key presents dismissed as a more formal alternative to fired.

items.pt: ser dispensado por extinção ou redução do posto
items.section: C · Not working and employment changes
items.example: Several employees were made redundant when the factory closed.
items.note: In UK work English, the post is no longer needed; not necessarily employee misconduct.

items.pt: ser dispensado; sofrer corte de pessoal
items.section: C · Not working and employment changes
items.example: Workers were laid off when orders fell sharply.
items.note: The book treats this as a less formal alternative to made redundant; duration and legal sense vary by region.

items.section: C · Not working and employment changes
items.example: She will take maternity leave shortly before her baby is born.
items.note: Time away from work around childbirth; be on maternity leave describes the ongoing state.

items.section: C · Not working and employment changes
items.example: Our colleague is on maternity leave until January.
items.note: State rather than action; a standard workplace explanation for an absence.

items.section: C · Not working and employment changes
items.example: He plans to take paternity leave after the birth.
items.note: Parental leave associated with a father or second parent; eligibility depends on local law.

items.pt: estar afastado por motivo de saúde
items.section: C · Not working and employment changes
items.example: The technician is on sick leave while recovering from surgery.
items.note: Time away from work because of illness or injury.

items.pt: tirar licença médica; afastar-se por doença
items.section: C · Not working and employment changes
items.example: She had to take sick leave for several weeks.
items.note: Leave is usually uncountable in this meaning.

items.section: C · Not working and employment changes
items.example: He chose to take early retirement before turning sixty.
items.note: Retire earlier than the usual or expected retirement age.

items.example: He is a workaholic who struggles to disconnect after office hours.
items.note: Usually critical or humorous: someone excessively devoted to work.

items.example: She was promoted to project manager last month.
items.note: Promotion means move to a higher position or rank.

items.example: He applied for a job in embedded software.
items.note: Use apply for + job or position; apply to + company.

items.example: The electrician checked the installation before the machine was switched on.
items.note: An illustrated skilled trade in Exercise 16.4, confirmed by the answer key.

items.example: Managers should delegate work instead of trying to do everything.
items.note: Exercise 16.2 uses work as a non-count noun after delegate.

items.pt: trabalho de meio período; atividade profissional de tempo parcial
items.example: She found part-time work editing a local magazine.
items.note: Exercise 16.5 uses part-time work for an offer of limited working hours.
